A swarm member: a built agent, or a registered @agent factory and its arguments.
Create one with member(), which documents the fields and the member contract.

Source

class Member(BaseModel)



agent Agent | None

A built, registered agent. Exactly one of agent and factory is set.

factory AgentFactory | None

A registered @agent factory, called with args to build the member’s agent.

args dict[str, Any]

The factory’s keyword arguments.

name str | None

The member’s name. None uses the agent’s or factory’s unqualified registry name.

role str | None

The member’s role, given to the controller and in the member’s preamble.

choose_name bool

Whether the member chooses its own name. True leaves the member’s name out of its preamble, which asks it to choose a name and tell the other members; the swarm still uses name for everything it records.

count int

How many members this record stands for. Above 1 needs the factory form.

limits list[Limit]

The member’s own limits.

bridged bool | None

Whether the member’s agent is bridged. None counts agents in the inspect_swe/ namespace as bridged.

sandbox str | None

The member’s own sandbox environment, where {member} stands for the member’s name. None shares the sample’s sandbox.

visible_sandboxes list[str]

Other sandbox environments the member can reach by name, such as a shared service. Only with sandbox.






The swarm-wide budget.
By default the swarm derives its caps from the sample’s cost, token and time limits when it starts, holding back reserve of each. The caps are stopping rules: when one is reached the swarm stops its members, gives them up to grace seconds to finish the calls they have in flight, and then cancels the members still running. If the sample has a time limit, the grace period is capped at half its remaining time.
Every field is a plain value, so each can be a task parameter, and two budgets that differ in any field are logged as different arguments.

Source

class Budget(BaseModel)



cost float | None

Swarm cost cap in dollars. None derives it from the sample’s cost limit.

tokens int | str | None

Swarm token cap. A string such as "output:1m" is parsed by parse_token_limit() and keeps its metering type. None derives it from the sample’s token limit, with that limit’s metering type.

time float | None

Seconds after which the swarm stops its members. None derives it from the sample’s time limit.

reserve float

Fraction of each sample limit held back when a cap is derived.

split Literal['pool', 'equal'] | tuple[float, ...]

How the cost and token caps are divided between members: one shared pool, equal shares, or one weight per member in roster order. A member that uses up its share stops, and its unused share is not given to the others.

grace float

Seconds members have, at most, to finish calls already in flight after a stop. If the sample has a time limit, this period is capped at half its remaining time.

title: Shared Memory
text:
shared_memory() gives the swarm one board of files that every member reads and writes with a shared_memory tool. The tool has the commands of Inspect’s memory() tool, over files under /shared_memory, and one more, append. Every write goes through the swarm as a record from the member that made it, so the log keeps the board’s whole history, and members hear about each other’s changes.
Members that get shared_memory also get swarm_wait, so a member that needs a peer’s work waits instead of polling. Each sample has its own board, which is gone when the swarm ends.
examples/shared_memory.py is a runnable swarm that splits a count between members, who share their parts on the board and wait for each other.

title: Shared Memory
Shared Memory
text:
The tool
The shared_memory tool’s commands are view, create, str_replace, insert, append, delete, rename and changes. Paths are /shared_memory followed by up to eight components of letters, digits, ., _ and -.

Each file has an id, such as f-3, which it keeps through renames. Status lines and swarm_wait results name files by id. view takes an id as file_id, in place of path. A view shows the file’s path, which the write commands take.
A file view shows the file inside a <peer_file> fence that names its id, path, version and last writer. A directory view lists every file under it at any depth, with its id, version and last writer.
Write commands return a short acknowledgment, not the file. View a file to see it.
Every result ends with a status line naming the files other agents changed since this loop last viewed them, such as Shared memory: 2 files changed since you last viewed them (f-2, f-9). It names at most 10 files and counts the rest, as in (f-1, ..., f-10, and 2 more). With the messages channel, a result in the member’s own loop then ends with its count of unread messages, when any remain.
changes returns the board’s status line, naming every changed file, or Shared memory: no files changed since you last viewed them., so a loop can check for news without viewing anything. Like the status line, it marks nothing seen. With messages, its result in a member’s own loop also ends with the unread count, when any remain.


Fences are labels
A fence is a label for the reader, not a security boundary. A member can write text that looks like a fence, another member’s file, or text the swarm writes, such as a status line. The swarm does not refuse or clean such text.
What holds:

Members see each other’s text only in tool results.
The record of the board comes from the swarm’s own events and ids, never from the text of a result (The record of the board).

An experiment that needs stronger guarantees, such as a study of members that deceive each other, needs a channel that provides them (Writing a channel).


The seen rule
A loop must view a file in its current version before it overwrites it with create, inserts into it, renames it or deletes it. A write to a file changed since the loop’s last view is refused with an error that names the file and its last writer, and the loop views it and retries. So no member overwrites a change it has not seen.
Two commands need no view:

str_replace fails unless old_str occurs exactly once in the file as it is when the write lands, so it is safe without one.
append adds text on a new line at the end of the file as it is when the write lands, and creates the file if needed. It suits a log or list that many members write to.

title: Shared Memory
text:
Hearing about changes
The swarm adds no messages to a member’s conversation. A member learns what other agents changed only through its tools:

The status line at the end of every shared_memory result. With the messages channel, a result in the member’s own loop then ends with its count of unread messages.
shared_memory(command="changes"), which returns the board’s status line, naming every changed file, to check for changes without viewing anything.
swarm_wait, which blocks until a file the member watches changes (Waiting for other members).

A changed file stays in the status line until the loop views it. A deleted file is listed only to a loop that previously viewed or wrote it, including a blind append. These lists hold counts, file ids and member names, never a file path or file contents.

title: Shared Memory
text:
Waiting for other members
swarm_wait blocks until there is something for the member to look at:

A file it watches has a change that the waiting agent did not write and has not viewed. It watches one file with file_id, a file or directory with path, or the whole board with neither. A subagent’s write counts, so a member can wait for its own subagents.
Another member has ended.

It returns at once if that is already so, and keeps returning while such a file stays unviewed. Its result names the changed files by id and the ended members by name and status, never file content: the member views a file to read it.
A wait also ends without news: when every member is waiting, has ended or has not started; when the swarm stops; when the member’s own agent finishes; or after timeout seconds. max_wait sets the longest wait and the default timeout, 600 seconds unless you change it, for example shared_memory(max_wait=300).
A wait is time inside a tool call. It counts towards the member’s time limit, the swarm’s time cap and the sample’s time and working limits. It makes no model call, so it adds no tokens, cost or steps. The metrics report each member’s waits, their time, and its idle_time: the seconds the member did nothing but wait (Analysis).
A swarm with only the filesystem channel, or channels=[], has no swarm_wait: there is nothing it could wake on.

title: Shared Memory
text:
Subagents
A member’s subagents read and write the board as the member. deepagent’s general() subagents, synchronous and background, and any nested loop given swarm_tools(), get the shared_memory and swarm_wait tools.
The member’s agent decides which subagents get swarm_tools(). deepagent’s general() inherits the member’s tools, so it gets the board. research() gets its own read-only tools instead, and has the board only when you pass research(extra_tools=[swarm_tools()]).

Their writes are records from the member. The evidence also names the loop that made each write or read, and marks a subagent’s as nested.
Each loop has its own view of the board: the seen rule and the status line apply to the loop that calls the tool.
A member’s subagents share its write rate, so they cannot multiply its write volume.
A subagent’s wait counts in the member’s wait_time but not its idle_time.

A deepagent member also has a private memory() of its own by default. Pass deepagent(memory=False) when the board should be its only memory tool.

title: Shared Memory
text:
The record of the board
The swarm logs the members’ writes, views and waits as InfoEvents with source inspect_swarm and type comm. Each is in the span of the tool call that made it:

sent: a write that reached the swarm, with its operation and payload, and why it was refused if it was.
delivered: a write applied to the board, with its commit sequence number and each file’s previous and new version. Replaying the delivered writes in sequence order rebuilds every version of the board.
read: a view, with each file’s version and the record that last wrote it, or a listing.
waited: a swarm_wait call, with what ended it and how long it took.

Each event names the member and the loop that acted. The metrics count these events for each member.

title: Shared Memory
Shared Memory
text:
Migrating from memory(instance=...)
Before this channel, a board shared on purpose was a memory() tool with an explicit instance in every member’s tools, memory(instance="board"), with the prompt saying it is shared. That still works, and it is a different channel: members’ ToolEvents record its use, with no sender, fence, status line, bounds or comm events. Nothing refuses using both; an arm that wants the board as its only channel gives no two members a shared instance.
To move a task to the channel:

In the member builder, replace memory(instance="board") with swarm_tools() in the tools. The builder stays a registered @agent.
For a deepagent member, pass memory=False to keep one memory tool as before, or leave deepagent’s private memory() as an extra notebook per member. These are different experimental conditions.
Replace the instructions that described the board with "shared_memory" or shared_memory(...) in channels=. Its instructions go in each member’s preamble.
Change the prompt’s tool and path names (memory, /memories) to shared_memory and /shared_memory.

What changes for the members:

Overwriting with create, insert, delete and rename need a current view (The seen rule), and append adds an entry at the end of a file without one.
Writes return an acknowledgment, not a snippet of the file.
A directory view lists every file under it at any depth, and there are no empty directories.
Paths are narrower, files and the board are bounded, and tabs are kept.
Views are fenced and name the last writer, and status lines report changes.

An eval set comparing the two boards runs them as two arms: the channel list and the builder’s arguments differ, so their task identifiers do. examples/proof_swarm.py is shaped like such a port: members with their own sandboxes whose only channel is the board.

title: Messages
text:
messages() lets members address each other. A member sends with send_message and reads what was sent to it with read_messages. list_members shows who is in the swarm and whether each member is still running. Every message goes through the swarm as a record from the member that sent it, so the log keeps who sent what to whom and when it was read.
The swarm adds no messages to a member’s conversation. A member hears about new messages only through its tools.

title: Messages
text:
Wiring
Members get the tools from swarm_tools(), as for Shared Memory. Call it inside a member builder registered with @agent:
from inspect_ai.agent import Agent, agent, react
from inspect_ai.tool import bash

from inspect_swarm import filesystem, member, messages, swarm, swarm_tools


@agent
def worker() -> Agent:
    return react(tools=[bash(), swarm_tools()])


solver = swarm(
    members=member(worker, count=4),
    channels=[filesystem(), messages()],
)

Only the member’s own loop gets the tools. Its subagents, such as a deepagent member’s general(), do not, so each inbox has one reader.
The channel can be combined with shared_memory(). Then the member’s own loop gets both channels’ tools and one swarm_wait for both.
The channel needs member names that start with a lowercase letter, followed by at most 47 lowercase letters, digits, _ or -. all and swarm are reserved.
Bridged members cannot use the channel yet, and swarm() refuses a bridged member beside it.

title: Messages
text:
The tools
send_message(to, message, reply_to=None, wake=True) sends a message and returns its id, such as Sent m-3 to worker-2.

to is a member name, a list of names, or "all" for every other running member.
reply_to is the id of a message the sender sent or read, which this one answers.
wake=False sends a message that does not end the recipient’s swarm_wait.

A send is refused, and reaches no one, when an address is not a running member other than the sender, or when one of the limits is passed. A message to a member that has ended, or has not started, is refused rather than kept.
read_messages() returns the member’s unread messages, oldest first, and marks them read:
2 messages, oldest first.

<peer_message id="m-9" from="worker-2" to="worker-1, worker-3">
...
</peer_message>
<peer_message id="m-14" from="worker-4" to="worker-1" reply_to="m-6">
...
</peer_message>
1 more unread message; call read_messages() again.
One read returns as many whole messages as fit in a bound set by max_bytes and the roster, and always at least one. The generate config’s max_tool_output does not apply to it, so a message is never cut. read_messages never waits; swarm_wait does.
list_members() lists the members in roster order, with each one’s role, its state (pending, running or ended) and, once it has ended, its status, such as submitted. It marks the caller with (you), and ends with the caller’s count of unread messages.

Fences are labels
As in Shared Memory, a fence is a label for the reader, not a security boundary. A message is delivered as it was typed, so a member can write text that looks like another member’s message or a status line. The record of messages comes from the swarm’s own events and ids, never from the text of a result.

title: Messages
text:
Hearing about messages
While a member has unread messages, the results of the swarm’s own tools in its own loop end with a line that counts them, such as You have 2 unread messages.: send_message, list_members, shared_memory and swarm_wait. list_members also says when there are none, so a member can call it to check for messages. A read_messages result says how many remain unread instead. The tools of other channels, yours or Inspect’s, carry no count. These lines hold counts only, never message text. Errors have no count: a member that gets one sees the count on its next result. A tool output limit smaller than the line can cut it, since the limit applies after the line is added. A member’s subagents cannot read its messages, so their results do not count them.
swarm_wait returns while the member has unread messages sent with wake=True, and names their senders: 2 unread messages (from worker-2, worker-4). Call read_messages() to read them. It keeps returning until the member reads them. A result with other news too, such as a changed file or an ended member, also ends with the count. Messages sent with wake=False do not end a wait, but a wait that returns for another reason counts them. It also returns when another member ends, when every member is waiting, has ended or has not started, when the swarm stops, or after timeout seconds, as described in Shared Memory. max_wait sets the longest wait, 120 seconds unless you change it. With shared_memory() too, the longer of the two channels’ max_wait applies.
A member busy in a long tool call hears nothing until the call ends.

title: Messages
text:
The record of messages
The swarm logs messages as InfoEvents with source inspect_swarm and type comm, each in the span of the tool call that made it:

sent: a send that reached the swarm, with its addresses, recipients, text, reply_to and wake, and why it was refused if it was. An inbox that is full, or a duplicate, is refused by the control admit.
delivered: a message delivered, with its recipients and commit sequence number.
read: a read_messages result, with the ids of the messages it showed. A read that showed nothing has no event.
waited: a swarm_wait call, with what ended it and the unread messages it named.

The metrics count these events for each member.
A native member’s calls to send_message and read_messages are ordinary tool calls, so Inspect Sentinel’s tool stages see them, as in Shared Memory.

title: Restrictions
text:
No background work in bridged members. A member cannot combine background work with the agent bridge. background() raises in a bridged member, and a member that uses the bridge after starting background work ends errored.
No channels with tools for bridged members. A bridged member cannot use the shared-memory channel yet, and swarm() refuses one beside it.
No checkpointing. Inspect’s sample checkpointing does not restore the swarm’s shared state or its caps, so a swarm raises an error before any member starts in a sample with checkpointing on. Turn checkpointing off for tasks that run a swarm: set checkpoint=False on Task() or eval(), or remove every checkpoint setting, including --checkpoint and INSPECT_EVAL_CHECKPOINT.
No ACP agents. ACP agents wait for their caller to drive them, so they are refused.
No scorers that read a member’s tool state. Each member runs in its own tool-state scope, so built-in tools that keep state in the store (memory(), bash_session(), web_browser(), the skill tool) keep each member’s at keys inside its scope, which differ from the default ones. Tool state that a setup solver prepared at the default instance is not carried into the members either; they start with fresh state (Members).

title: Restrictions
text:
Bridged members
A bridged member runs a CLI agent in the sandbox through Inspect’s agent bridge. inspect_swe agents count as bridged by default; pass member(..., bridged=True) for other agents that use the bridge. The swarm stops a bridged member by cancelling it.
The CLI’s own tool calls do not emit Inspect ToolEvents, so the tool-event evidence described here does not cover them, Inspect Sentinel does not see them, and longest_identical_tool_run is null for bridged members.

title: Restrictions
text:
What the log records

Members’ ToolEvents are the record of what they did, except for bridged members.
The shared-memory channel’s writes, views and waits are comm events (Shared Memory).
Files members share in a sandbox, tool instances they share, and a tool that reads the transcript are channels the swarm observes but does not record (Channels).

Spans inside a swarm log no StoreEvents. The swarm’s span logs the net change to the store, which says what changed but not which member changed it. If an error, limit or cancellation escapes the swarm and ends the sample, the log may have no StoreEvent for the swarm’s writes. sample.store is always the record of the final store.

title: Restrictions
text:
The store keys
The swarm owns three keys in the sample store, written when the swarm ends: inspect_swarm:result_id, inspect_swarm:ledger and inspect_swarm:metrics. Task code must not write them, or an event with source inspect_swarm. The result record itself is an event in the transcript (Scoring). A tool that reads the transcript sees every member’s model and tool calls, a channel between members that the swarm records no evidence of (Scoring).

title: Inspect Swarm
text:
Inspect Swarm runs a swarm of agents on one sample of an Inspect task. A swarm is an Inspect agent, so it replaces the task’s solver, and the task’s scorer scores the swarm’s answer.

title: Inspect Swarm
text:
Getting Started
Install it from PyPI:
pip install inspect_swarm
or, in a uv project:
uv add inspect_swarm
To install the latest development version from GitHub:
pip install git+https://github.com/meridianlabs-ai/inspect_swarm
or, in a uv project:
uv add "inspect_swarm @ git+https://github.com/meridianlabs-ai/inspect_swarm"
It needs inspect_ai 0.3.283 or later and Python 3.11 or later.

title: Inspect Swarm
section: Run a swarm on an existing task
text:
Run a swarm on an existing task
Pass swarm() as the solver. From Python:
from inspect_ai import eval
from inspect_ai.agent import react

from inspect_swarm import member, swarm

from my_tasks import my_task

eval(
    my_task(),
    solver=swarm(members=member(react, count=4)),
    model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5",
)
From the command line:
inspect eval my_tasks.py --solver inspect_swarm/swarm -S 'members={factory: react, count: 4}'
Each sample runs four react() members, react-1 to react-4, at the same time. Each starts with the sample’s input and a short preamble: its name, the number of members, and how to share files. The swarm stops at the first submission and uses it as its answer. The other members finish the calls they have in flight and stop. The task’s scorer scores the answer as it would score a single agent.
--solver and eval(solver=...) replace the task’s whole solver, including any system message or tools it set up, so give the members their tools and prompt. Members use the eval’s model unless they are given one. The task’s setup solver still runs first.

title: Inspect Swarm
text:
A task with a swarm
A task can build the swarm itself. This one, from examples/getting_started.py, makes the number of members a task parameter:
from inspect_ai import Task, task
from inspect_ai.agent import react
from inspect_ai.scorer import match
from questions import QUESTIONS

from inspect_swarm import member, swarm


@task
def getting_started(k: int = 3) -> Task:
    return Task(
        dataset=QUESTIONS,
        solver=swarm(members=member(react, count=k), channels=[]),
        scorer=match(),
        token_limit=200_000,
    )
inspect eval examples/getting_started.py --model openai/gpt-5-mini -T k=4

channels=[] gives the members no channel. The default, filesystem, tells members to share files in the sample’s sandbox, and these questions have none. See Channels.
The swarm takes its budget from the sample’s limits: here it stops its members at 95% of the token limit. See Budgets.
-T k=1 is a swarm of one, the single-agent arm to compare with. See Scoring.

title: Inspect Swarm
text:
What the log shows
Each member’s events are in a timeline named after it, so the log viewer can show one member’s trajectory. The sample’s messages are its input followed by the answer’s message. When the swarm ends, it writes its result record to the transcript: each member’s state and status, and which member’s output is the answer. Read it with swarm_result(); see Scoring. It also writes two entries to the sample store:

inspect_swarm:ledger: the swarm’s caps and the usage and cost of each member. See Analysis.
inspect_swarm:metrics: tokens, cost and time for the swarm and each member, and counts of how members acted and communicated. See Analysis.

title: Inspect Swarm

Learning more

Members: member records, names, limits, member builders, and how a member ends.
Controllers: when the swarm stops, and writing a controller of your own.
Channels and Shared Memory: how members share information, and waiting for each other.
Budgets and Sandboxes: the swarm’s caps and splits, and shared or per-member sandboxes.
Scoring, Analysis and Restrictions: the answer and the result record, metrics, the ledger, and what the swarm does not support or record.

The examples are runnable tasks for each of these. The designs behind the swarm are in design/.

title: Channels
text:
channels= decides how members share information. There are three built-in channels:

filesystem, the default: a convention for sharing files in a sandbox, stated in each member’s preamble. It adds no tools.
shared_memory: a board of files that members read and write with a tool, with a record of every write and read. See Shared Memory.
messages: direct messages between members, with a record of every message and read. See Messages.

channels=[] gives members no channel instructions. Channels change what members are told and what tools they get, not what they can reach: members share the sample’s sandbox whatever the channels, unless they have their own (Sandboxes).
A channel is given as an object, filesystem(...), or by its registered name with its default arguments, "filesystem". Each channel can be given once.

title: Channels
text:
The filesystem channel
filesystem tells each member, in its preamble, to share files in /shared, to read and append to /shared/notes.md, and to keep its own work in /scratch/<member>. It does not create these directories. Change the paths with filesystem(...):
from inspect_ai.agent import react

from inspect_swarm import filesystem, member, swarm

solver = swarm(
    members=member(react, count=4),
    channels=[filesystem(shared="/work/shared", scratch="/work/{member}")],
)
A member that chooses its own name (Members) is told to keep its work in /scratch/<your name>, a directory named with the name it chose, and to check that no other member uses the same one. The members you named are still told /scratch/<member>, and, when any member chooses, that a member that chooses could pick the same directory, so they check that no other member uses it.
When members have their own sandboxes and each sandbox mounts one shared volume, use filesystem(shared_volume=True). Set shared= to the absolute path where the volume is mounted; notes= must be inside it. The preamble then says that shared and the notes file in it are the same in every member’s sandbox, and gives no scratch directory, since each sandbox is already private. The swarm cannot check that the volume is mounted, and it refuses shared_volume=True when members share the sample’s sandbox. See Sandboxes.
examples/shared_sandbox.py runs bash() members in one container with this channel.

title: Channels
section: Shared files are observed, not recorded
text:
Shared files are observed, not recorded
The filesystem channel opens no state and offers no tools, so no tool of the swarm’s carries file traffic. What the log has is each member’s own tool calls (bash(), python(), text_editor()), as ToolEvents.
Those tool calls are evidence that members may have communicated through files, not a complete record. Processes a member starts in the sandbox can read and write files between logged tool calls, and after the member has ended. A bridged member’s file operations are the CLI’s own tools, which leave no ToolEvent at all. An experiment that attributes communication to the filesystem must state this limit, or add its own instrumentation, such as filesystem snapshots or audit logs in the sandbox.
The same holds for every other path between members that the swarm does not carry:

A built-in tool given the same explicit instance in several members, such as memory(instance="board"), shares its state through the sample store. Members’ ToolEvents record its use, and nothing else does. See Members.
A tool that reads the transcript sees the other members’ model and tool calls (Scoring).

Channels limit what members are told, not what they can do. An arm meant to have one channel only, or none, needs members that cannot reach each other otherwise: their own sandboxes, and no shared tool instances.

title: Channels
Members
text:
A member is an agent registered with @agent, such as react() or deepagent(). Give it in one of two forms:

The factory form: the factory and its arguments, member(react, args={...}). The swarm calls the factory once for each member in each sample, so every member gets its own agent. count makes several members from one record.
The built form: an agent you have built, member(react(...)), or the agent alone. It is one member. The same agent object cannot be in two members.

from inspect_ai.agent import deepagent, react
from inspect_ai.tool import bash, python
from inspect_ai.util import token_limit

from inspect_swarm import member, swarm

solver = swarm(
    members=[
        member(
            react,
            args={"tools": [bash(), python()]},
            name="solver",
            role="solve the task",
            count=3,
        ),
        member(
            deepagent(tools=[bash()]),
            name="reviewer",
            role="check the solvers' work in /shared",
            limits=[token_limit(200_000)],
        ),
    ],
)
This swarm has four members: solver-1 to solver-3 and reviewer. The role is added to the member’s preamble and given to the controller.

title: Members
text:
Names
A member is named after its agent (react, deepagent) unless you give name. With count above 1 the members are name-1 to name-k. Names must be unique in the swarm. They cannot be init, solvers or scorers, and cannot contain / or #. The shared-memory channel also needs names that start with a lowercase letter, followed by at most 47 lowercase letters, digits, _ or -.
Members left on their default name are numbered across the whole roster, not per record. So one member with a different prompt and model takes two records:
from inspect_ai.agent import react

from inspect_swarm import member, swarm

solver = swarm(
    members=[
        member(react, args={"prompt": "Solve the task."}, count=6),
        member(
            react,
            args={
                "prompt": "Check the others' work in /shared.",
                "model": "openai/gpt-5",
            },
        ),
    ],
)
The first record makes react-1 to react-6 and the second react-7.
When every copy differs, give each its own record. A list comprehension builds them:
prompts = ["Try algebra.", "Try brute force.", "Try a proof by cases."]
solver = swarm(members=[member(react, args={"prompt": p}) for p in prompts])
These are react-1 to react-3. Names you give with name are not numbered across records, so give each record its own.

Members that choose their names
With choose_name=True a member is not told its name. Its preamble says how many agents are in the swarm and asks it to choose a name for itself and tell the other members what it is:
from inspect_ai.agent import react
from inspect_ai.tool import bash

from inspect_swarm import member, swarm

solver = swarm(
    members=member(react, args={"tools": [bash()]}, count=4, choose_name=True),
)
Each member starts with You are one of 4 agents in a swarm working on this task at the same time. Choose a name for yourself and tell the other members what it is. Its role, if it has one, is still stated. The log still names the members react-1 to react-4: the swarm’s timelines, spans, tool state, budget shares and result record use those names. The name a member chose is in its transcript, not in the swarm’s records.
A roster can mix the two, for example a lead you name and workers that name themselves. The filesystem channel then tells every member that its scratch directory may be taken by another member (Channels).
A swarm in which any member chooses its name can use only the filesystem channel or no channel (channels=[]). Other channels, including shared memory and your own, show members to each other by name, so swarm() refuses them.
The swarm does not change text you give the member yourself: the sample input, a controller’s start(input=...), the agent’s prompt, and the sandbox configuration.

title: Members
text:
Limits
limits takes token, cost, turn, message and time limits for that member alone. Working limits are refused. A member that reaches one ends with status member_limit:<type>, and the others continue. The swarm’s own caps are set with budget= (Budgets).

title: Members
text:
Member builders
A member builder is a function registered with @agent that builds the member’s agent. Pass it to member() without calling it, with its arguments in args:
from inspect_ai.agent import Agent, agent, react
from inspect_ai.tool import bash

from inspect_swarm import member, shared_memory, swarm, swarm_tools


@agent
def worker() -> Agent:
    return react(tools=[bash(), swarm_tools()])


solver = swarm(members=member(worker, name="w", count=3), channels=[shared_memory()])
Use a builder for anything the swarm gives a member at run time, such as swarm_tools() (Shared Memory). The log records a builder by its name and arguments, so the swarm can be rebuilt from the log. It cannot rebuild swarm_tools() passed in args or inside an agent you built.
A builder is also the place for anything each member must have its own of. Every member built from one record gets the same objects from args, and two built agents given the same tool object share it, across members and samples. Inspect’s built-in tools keep their state in the sample store or the sandbox, so this matters only for a custom tool or helper that keeps state in its Python object (a counter, a cache, a client). The swarm calls a builder once for each member in each sample, so what the builder creates belongs to one member. examples/stop_on_proof.py keeps a per-member flag this way.

title: Members
text:
Tool state
Each member runs in its own tool-state scope, named after the member. Built-in tools that keep state in the sample store (memory(), bash_session(), web_browser(), the skill tool) give each member its own state when their instance is left at the default, so the default memory() is private to each member.
An explicit instance is used as given: members that name the same instance share its state. A board shared on purpose was memory(instance="board") before the shared-memory channel; see Shared Memory for moving to the channel.

The sample store itself is shared. State that custom tools or agent code keep in the store with no instance is shared unless they resolve their instance with tool_state_instance().
Tool state that a setup solver prepared at the default instance before the swarm runs is not visible to the members. They start with fresh state.

title: Members
text:
Background work
Native members support deepagent(background=True) and integer background limits. Work started with background() belongs to its member and uses its limits, share and sandbox. A member limit or swarm cap ends the background task that reached it. A swarm cap also starts the swarm’s soft stop; other work gets the effective grace period to finish calls already in flight.
When the member’s agent ends, its background work gets the swarm’s grace period to finish work in flight. The swarm then cancels the rest and waits for its cleanup before the member ends. Budget.grace=0 skips the grace wait. A controller therefore sees a member’s end only after this drain.
Start background work from the running agent, not its factory. A factory that starts it makes the member errored. Work started outside background() (an asyncio task, a process left running in the sandbox) is not stopped.

title: Members
text:
How a member ends
A member’s status says how it ended:



Status
Meaning




submitted
Its agent returned normally. Its output is its answer.


unsubmitted
Its agent returned with a content_filter or model_length stop reason, as react() does after repeated refusals or a context overflow.


stopped
The swarm stopped it, for example when another member submitted or the swarm’s time cap was reached.


share
It used up its share of a split budget.


member_limit:<type>
It reached one of its own limits.


member_limit:custom
Its agent stopped itself by raising LimitExceededError("custom", ...) with no source, for example from react(on_continue=...). The other members continue.


swarm_cap
Its call reached one of the swarm’s caps.


cancelled
It was cancelled, after the grace period of a stop or from outside the swarm.


errored
It raised any other error. The error ends the sample.



A normal return counts as a submission for any agent other than react()’s two cases above. An agent that gives up in some other way and returns is treated as having answered. To make a normal return mean something stronger, such as a passed check, have the member’s builder raise a custom limit when it is not so (Controllers).

title: Members
text:
A swarm of one
swarm(members=react(), channels=[]) is a single agent run under the swarm’s rules, with the same records. Use it as the single-agent arm when you compare a swarm with one agent (Scoring). Unlike a plain agent, it returns an empty output when its member does not submit.

title: Members
text:
Agents the swarm refuses

ACP agents wait for their caller to drive them, so they are refused.
Bridged members, which run a CLI agent in the sandbox through Inspect’s agent bridge, cannot have background work and cannot use channels with tools yet. See Restrictions.

title: Scoring
text: A swarm is scored by the task’s own scorers. The swarm is the task’s solver, so the scorers run after it, on the swarm’s output and on whatever the members left in the sandbox, as they would after a single agent. Inspect Swarm adds no scorer of its own; it records what the swarm did, so analysis can read it beside the scores.

title: Scoring
text: A swarm is scored by the task’s own scorers. The swarm is the task’s solver, so the scorers run after it, on the swarm’s output and on whatever the members left in the sandbox, as they would after a single agent. Inspect Swarm adds no scorer of its own; it records what the swarm did, so analysis can read it beside the scores.

title: Scoring
section: The answer and the result record
text:
The answer and the result record

The answer
The controller’s final rule chooses the swarm’s answer from the members’ submissions:

first, the default: the member that submitted earliest, by the swarm’s clock, with ties broken by roster order.
last: the latest submission, again with ties broken by roster order. leaderless(stop_on_submission=False, final="last") gives it, for a team whose members build on each other’s work (Controllers).

A controller of your own can also choose the answer itself, with choose_answer(), in place of the rule (Controllers). A member that ended any other way than submitting is never chosen (Members). When no member submitted, the answer is empty.
The swarm’s output is the chosen member’s ModelOutput, unchanged, so the scorer sees what it would have seen had that member run alone. The sample’s messages are its input followed by the answer’s message, whose metadata["inspect_swarm"] names the mode and the chosen member. Each member’s own conversation is in its timeline.


The result record
When the swarm ends, it writes a record of what it did to the transcript, as an evidence event in the swarm’s span. Read it with swarm_result(state) in a scorer, or swarm_result(sample) for a sample read from a log, which needs the sample’s events and attachments. The record is:
{
  "version": 1,
  "members": [
    {"name": "react-1", "role": null, "choose_name": false, "state": "ended", "status": "submitted", "submitted": true, "time": 41.2, "sandbox": null, "gate_checks": 0, "gate_passes": 0, "first_pass_time": null},
    {"name": "react-2", "role": null, "choose_name": false, "state": "ended", "status": "swarm_cap", "submitted": false, "time": 57.9, "sandbox": null, "gate_checks": 0, "gate_passes": 0, "first_pass_time": null}
  ],
  "final": {"mode": "first", "member": "react-1", "reason": null, "provisional": false}
}

A member’s state is pending (never started), running or ended, and status says how it ended (Members).
time is seconds from the swarm’s start to the member’s end.
choose_name is true for a member that chose its own name (Members). name is still the swarm’s name for it; the name it chose is in its transcript.
sandbox is the member’s own sandbox, or null when it shares the sample’s.
gate_checks, gate_passes and first_pass_time count the member’s in-loop checks (Checks during the run).
final.mode is first, last or controller, and final.member names the chosen member. Under controller, final.reason is the reason the controller gave. With no submission, mode and member are null and final.reason is "no_submissions".

The event adds "type": "result_record" and an "id", which the swarm also puts in the sample store under inspect_swarm:result_id, so that swarm_result() finds the record of the store it is given. If a limit, error or cancellation ends the swarm before it finalises its answer, the record has the answer so far with provisional: true, and that submission is the sample’s output: the first submission so far, the latest under last, or the controller’s choice once it has made one.
swarm_result() returns None when no swarm ran in the sample. It raises ValueError for a sample it cannot read the record of: one read without its events or attachments, one written by an inspect_swarm that kept the record in the store under inspect_swarm:result, or one that holds a swarm’s events but whose store names no record, as for a sample recovered from a crashed eval.


The record belongs to the swarm
Only the swarm writes the record and inspect_swarm:result_id. Task code (tools, member builders, controllers, scorers) must not write that key or an event with source inspect_swarm. Member names, roles and sandboxes, and a controller’s choose_answer() reason, must be text that a log keeps as it is: not beginning with attachment:// or tc://, which a log reads as a reference to an attachment, not a base64 data: URI, which a log removes when images are not logged, and valid UTF-8. The swarm does not write a record that holds such text, and its end raises ValueError.
There is no record while the swarm runs, so no member can read another’s results from it. A scorer that reads it after the swarm is how a task finds each member’s sandbox (Per-member sandboxes). A tool that reads the transcript sees every member’s model and tool calls anyway. That is a channel between members outside the swarm’s channels, and the swarm records no evidence of it.

title: Scoring
text:
Scoring what members leave
A scorer that reads the sandbox, rather than the answer, scores what every member left there. With the default leaderless, the swarm stops the other members at the first submission, so what they were doing is left half done. When the scorer reads a shared artifact, let every member run to its end with leaderless(stop_on_submission=False) (Controllers). The swarm returns after every member and its background work have ended, so the scorer sees the sandbox as the members left it.
examples/shared_sandbox.py scores a script that the members build together in a shared container.

title: Scoring
text:
Per-member sandboxes
With per-member sandboxes, the scorer still runs outside every member, where sandbox() is the sample’s default. A scorer that grades the members’ work names each member’s sandbox. The result record says which member used which, so the scorer can read it rather than repeat the roster:
@scorer(metrics=[accuracy()])
def tests_pass() -> Scorer:
    """Run the task's tests in each member's sandbox."""

    async def score(state: TaskState, target: Target) -> Score | None:
        # the record exists once the swarm has ended; a member's react(attempts=...)
        # or live control scoring calls this scorer during the solve
        if not state.completed:
            return None
        record = swarm_result(state)
        assert record is not None, "the task's solver is a swarm"
        passed = [
            m.name
            for m in record.members
            if (await sandbox(m.sandbox).exec(["sh", "/tests/run.sh"])).success
        ]
        return Score(value=CORRECT if passed else INCORRECT, metadata={"passed": passed})

    return score
A check can also run in a shared service rather than in each member’s sandbox. examples/proof_swarm.py mounts each member’s /workspace read-only in a comparator service, at /answers/<member>, and checks an answer there with one command:
async def run_check(member_sandbox: str) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """Check the answer a member left in its sandbox, with the comparator: whether it is a proof, and why."""
    result = await sandbox("comparator").exec(
        ["python3", "-c", VERIFY, f"/answers/{member_sandbox}/answer.txt"],
        timeout=60,
    )
    return result.success, result.stdout.strip() or result.stderr.strip()
VERIFY exits 0 only for a proof. Its scorer, any_member_proved(), calls run_check() for every member in the result record. A member that wrote a valid answer but was stopped before it submitted still passes, which is why the scorer grades every member’s work rather than only the chosen member’s.

title: Scoring
text:
Checks during the run
A task’s scorer can also run inside a member, as react(attempts=...) runs it on each submission. For each member, the swarm counts these checks of its own submissions, made in its own loop with the task’s first scorer:

gate_checks: how many submissions were checked.
gate_passes: how many of those passed, a score of 1.0 under Inspect’s default value_to_float().
first_pass_time: the swarm time of the first pass.

They are in the result record and the metrics. A member with its own score_value can pass its own gate where the count does not, since the count assumes the default converter. Inside a member, a scorer’s sandbox() is the member’s own.
A scorer that runs during the solve, under react(attempts=...), the other attempt loops or live control scoring, cannot read the result record: swarm_result() raises while a swarm in the sample runs. Such a scorer returns None until state.completed is True, as the per-member sandboxes example does. Inspect drops a None score, so the task also needs a scorer that returns a value during the solve, since an attempt loop fails when it gets no score. List that scorer first: the swarm counts checks from the task’s first scorer.

title: Scoring
text:
Comparisons
The swarm’s score is the task’s scorer on the swarm’s answer, or on what the members left for a scorer that reads the sandbox. Compare it with:

A single agent at the same budget. A swarm of one, swarm(members=agent, channels=[]), runs one agent under the swarm’s rules with the same records (Members), so both arms have a ledger. Unlike a plain agent, it returns an empty output when its member does not submit.
Epochs of a single agent, through Inspect’s own reducers on the task’s scorer, such as mean, max and pass_at_k:

from inspect_ai import Epochs, Task, task
from inspect_ai.agent import react
from inspect_ai.scorer import match
from questions import QUESTIONS

from inspect_swarm import swarm


@task
def single_agent() -> Task:
    return Task(
        dataset=QUESTIONS,
        solver=swarm(members=react(), channels=[]),
        scorer=match(),
        epochs=Epochs(4, ["mean", "pass_at_4"]),
        token_limit=50_000,
    )
pass_at_k and max choose with knowledge of the target, and the swarm’s answer rule does not, so they are upper references, not like-for-like comparisons.
Compare arms on the cost the log records, not on the caps (Analysis). team@k, the mean member and best@k on graded scores need each member’s own score, which Inspect Swarm does not record yet; best@k can be computed from per-epoch values in samples_df().

title: Controllers
text: controller= decides which members start, when and with what input, and when the swarm is done. It also decides which submission is the swarm’s answer: by a rule, first (the default) or last, or by choosing a member itself (Scoring).

title: Controllers
text: controller= decides which members start, when and with what input, and when the swarm is done. It also decides which submission is the swarm’s answer: by a rule, first (the default) or last, or by choosing a member itself (Scoring).

title: Controllers
text:
leaderless
The only built-in controller is leaderless, the default. It starts every member with the sample’s input and stops the swarm when the first member submits, since that submission is the answer. The other members finish the calls they have in flight and stop. Those still running after the grace period are cancelled. If no member submits, the swarm ends when all have ended.
Pass leaderless(stop_on_submission=False) to let every member run to its end:
from inspect_ai.agent import react

from inspect_swarm import leaderless, member, swarm

solver = swarm(
    members=member(react, count=4),
    controller=leaderless(stop_on_submission=False),
)
Use it when:

The scorer reads what members leave in the sandbox, where members still working change what is scored (Scoring).
You measure each member’s result, as for team@k.
Your agent returns normally when it gives up, which would count as a submission and stop the swarm.

The answer is still the first submission. When the members work as a team and the latest submission should be the answer, add final="last":
from inspect_swarm import leaderless

controller = leaderless(stop_on_submission=False, final="last")
final="last" needs stop_on_submission=False, and leaderless refuses it otherwise.
leaderless returns the stop reason submitted when a submission stopped the swarm and all_done when every member ended. The ledger records it as stop_reason (Analysis).

title: Controllers
text:
Writing a controller
A controller is a factory decorated with @swarm_controller that returns a Controller. Its run function is called once per sample with a SwarmControl, through which it starts members and receives their events. It returns a stop reason, and returning requests the stop.
from collections.abc import Sequence
from contextlib import aclosing

from inspect_swarm import (
    Controller,
    MemberInfo,
    StopReason,
    SwarmControl,
    swarm_controller,
)


@swarm_controller
def escalate(first: str = "fast") -> Controller:
    """Start one member; start the others only if it ends without a submission."""

    def check(roster: Sequence[MemberInfo]) -> None:
        if first not in [m.name for m in roster]:
            raise ValueError(f"escalate(): no member is named {first!r}.")

    async def run(swarm: SwarmControl) -> StopReason:
        swarm.start(first)
        async with aclosing(swarm.events()) as events:
            async for event in events:
                if event.submitted:
                    return "submitted"
        for m in swarm.members:
            if m.state == "pending":
                swarm.start(m)
        async with aclosing(swarm.events()) as events:
            async for event in events:
                if event.submitted:
                    return "submitted"
        return "all_done"

    return Controller(run, check=check)

swarm.members are the members in roster order, as MemberHandles: name, role, state (pending, running or ended), status and whether it submitted. A controller never sees what a member wrote.
swarm.start(member, input=None) starts a member and returns at once. input replaces the swarm’s input for that member; None gives it the swarm’s input. The member’s preamble follows either. A member runs once, and starting one after the stop has begun raises.
swarm.events() yields each event once, in order from the swarm’s start. Its only kind is MemberEnded, with the member’s name, status and whether it submitted. The iterator ends when no member is running and no event is waiting, so a member started later needs a new events() call. Use one iterator at a time, and close it, as aclosing() does here.
check, if given, is called with the roster when swarm() is called. Raise ValueError for a roster the controller cannot run.
final, if given, is the rule that chooses the answer: first (the default, as here) or last.
The stop reasons all_done, submitted, verified and quiescence are recorded as they are. Any other is recorded as controller:<reason>.

A Controller holds configuration only: one object serves every sample, so keep per-sample state in run’s local variables. The factory’s arguments are logged with the controller, so it can be rebuilt from the log. Pass the controller to the swarm, swarm(..., controller=escalate("fast")), or by its registered name with its default arguments, controller="escalate".

Choosing the answer
A controller can choose the answer itself. swarm.choose_answer(member, reason=None) names a member that has ended with a submission, and its submission is then the answer, whatever the final rule says. A controller chooses once. The record gives the mode controller and the reason (Scoring).
This controller answers with the first submission from a member with a given role, and falls back to the final rule, first, when none of them submits:
from contextlib import aclosing

from inspect_swarm import Controller, StopReason, SwarmControl, swarm_controller


@swarm_controller
def prefer(role: str) -> Controller:
    """Answer with the first submission from a member with this role, if any."""

    async def run(swarm: SwarmControl) -> StopReason:
        for m in swarm.members:
            swarm.start(m)
        chosen = False
        async with aclosing(swarm.events()) as events:
            async for event in events:
                if (
                    not chosen
                    and event.submitted
                    and swarm.member(event.member).role == role
                ):
                    swarm.choose_answer(event.member, reason=f"first {role} to submit")
                    chosen = True
        return "all_done"

    return Controller(run)

title: Controllers
text:
Stopping on the first proof
Some tasks have a checker, such as a proof checker or a test suite, and the experiment wants to stop when the first member’s answer passes it. examples/stop_on_proof.py has such a controller:
from contextlib import aclosing

from inspect_swarm import Controller, StopReason, SwarmControl, swarm_controller


@swarm_controller
def until_proved() -> Controller:
    """Start every member, and stop the swarm when the first one ends `submitted`.

    Valid only when a member's normal return means a passed check, as `checked_solver()` makes it.
    """

    async def run(swarm: SwarmControl) -> StopReason:
        for m in swarm.members:
            swarm.start(m)
        async with aclosing(swarm.events()) as events:
            async for event in events:
                if event.submitted:
                    return "proved"
        return "all_done"

    return Controller(run)
It records the stop reason controller:proved. But it is right only under a precondition: a member’s normal return must mean that its answer passed the check. A react() member also returns normally when it runs out of attempts, after three refusals, or after a context overflow it could not recover from. Without the precondition, until_proved can stop every member on a member that gave up, and record controller:proved with nothing proved.
The member’s builder makes the precondition hold. It raises a member-local custom limit when its agent returns without a passing check, which ends that member as member_limit:custom while the others continue:
from inspect_ai.agent import Agent, AgentAttempts, AgentState, agent, react
from inspect_ai.scorer import Value, value_to_float
from inspect_ai.util import LimitExceededError


@agent
def checked_solver(attempts: int = 5) -> Agent:
    """A `react()` member that returns normally only when one of its submissions passed the task's scorer."""
    passed = False
    to_float = value_to_float()

    def score_value(value: Value) -> float:
        nonlocal passed
        result = to_float(value)
        passed = passed or result == 1.0
        return result

    inner = react(attempts=AgentAttempts(attempts, score_value=score_value))

    async def execute(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
        state = await inner(state)
        if not passed:
            # with no `source`, this ends only this member, as member_limit:custom
            raise LimitExceededError(
                "custom",
                value=0,
                limit=0,
                message="returned without a passing check",
            )
        return state

    return execute

The check here is the task’s own scorer, which react(attempts=...) runs on each submission but the last. A last submission is never checked, so it is not a proof, and attempts must be at least 2 for any submission to be checked.
The builder is called once for each member in each sample, so passed belongs to one member.
With this builder, the default leaderless would stop at the first proof too, recording submitted rather than controller:proved.
With background work, a controller sees a member’s end only after the member’s background work has drained (Members), so the other members stop up to one grace period later.

examples/proof_swarm.py uses the same controller with per-member sandboxes and a checking service in its own container. Its member builder checks the answer the member leaves when the agent returns, not only the checks the agent asked for, since a member could pass a check and then change its answer.

When the swarm ends it writes two entries to the sample store, each also logged as an InfoEvent with source inspect_swarm:

title: Analysis
text:
Metrics
For the swarm:

tokens, cost: everything in the swarm: members, controller and final step.
wall_clock: seconds from the swarm’s start to its end.
never_acted: members with no completed model call.
steps_to_answer: completed model calls of the member whose output is the answer, null with no answer.
longest_member_steps: the largest number of completed model calls of any member.
critical_steps_to_answer: the number of completed model calls on the longest chain of calls the answer depended on, across members (The critical path).

Step counts include cache replays and exclude failed or cancelled attempts. A member’s subagents’ calls count as the member’s. steps_to_answer and longest_member_steps bound each member’s own sequential depth from above, not the swarm’s: they do not see that one member waited for or read another’s work.
For each member, in roster order:

tokens, cost: its usage, its subagents’ and background work’s included.
running_time: seconds from its start to its end, null for a member never started.
longest_identical_tool_run: the longest run of identical tool calls (same function and arguments), a sign of a stuck member. null for a bridged member, whose tool calls leave no tool events.
gate_checks, gate_passes, first_pass_time: its in-loop checks (Scoring).
comm, waits, waits_by_outcome, wait_time, idle_time: below.


The critical path
critical_steps_to_answer is the measure to read latency by: how many model calls the answer took one after another, given that members work in parallel but wait on and build on each other. A member that waits for a peer’s file and then answers in three steps has steps_to_answer 3, but if the peer took ten steps to write that file, the answer took at least 11.
Each member’s calls, its subagents’ and background work’s included, form one chain in the order they began. Chains link between members in two ways:

A view of a shared_memory file, or a swarm_wait result that names a file, follows the writes it showed. A view of a file follows every write in its history; a view of a deleted file follows the delete. Directory listings and the changes status line make no link.
A swarm_wait result that names a member’s end follows all of that member’s calls.

A wait that also reached a custom waiting channel links no files, since its evidence does not say which channel named them. Its links to member ends count either way.
The chain ends when the answering member ends, after its background work has finished, since that work can still change the member’s output.
The number over-counts work inside a member. Parallel and background subagents, tool calls of one turn, and any other concurrent work count one after another, and the answering member’s background work after its agent returned, its reads included, counts whether or not it changed the answer. That excess reaches peers through the member’s later writes.
The number also misses links. Only shared_memory and swarm_wait make them, so information that members share in other ways adds none: messages, a shared sandbox, a shared volume, a service, a custom channel and its wait results, a shared tool or store key, or a controller that passes one member’s result to another. A swarm_wait result that reports more than ten files names only the first ten in its evidence, so the rest make no link until the member views them. Missed links can only lower the number.
With both effects it is not a bound on true causal depth in either direction. A nested swarm’s board makes no link for the outer swarm; its own metrics count it.
It is null when there is no answer, when the answering member has no recorded end, when the board’s evidence is inconsistent (with a warning in the log), and for a sample resumed from a checkpoint. Metrics written by earlier versions do not have it.


Communication
Each member’s comm has an entry, by channel name, for each channel with records, such as shared_memory:

records and record_bytes: its writes or messages delivered to the channel, and their size.
rejections: its writes or messages the swarm refused, by the control that refused them, such as rate.
reads and listings: its views of files and of directories, and its read_messages results that showed messages.

A member’s subagents count as the member. Every member has an entry for every such channel the swarm opened, zeros included. A swarm with none (filesystem only, or channels=[]) has comm {} for every member: communication through files is observed, not recorded, so it is not reported as zero (Channels).


Waits
Each member’s metrics count its swarm_wait calls, its subagents’ included:

waits: the number of waits.
waits_by_outcome: that number by what ended each wait: news (a changed file or an ended member), all_waiting, stopping, member_ending, timeout or cancelled. An outcome that ended no wait is left out.
wait_time: the waits’ total seconds. Waits of a member’s subagents that overlap each count.
idle_time: the seconds the member did nothing but wait: its own agent in swarm_wait, not yet released, and none of its background work running. A subagent’s wait adds to wait_time but not to idle_time.

In a swarm with no swarm_wait (filesystem only, or channels=[]) the four are null, so 0 means the wait was offered and unused. Waiting is wall-clock time, so a member’s running_time includes it.


Wiring checks
The metrics also check that members are wired to the channels. tools_unwired lists, in a swarm with a channel that has tools, the members with a completed model call whose loops never resolved swarm_tools(). A member listed there did not get what the channel offers, so it ran a different experiment from the one configured.

title: Analysis
text:
Samples dataframe
inspect_swarm.analysis.SwarmColumns adds each sample’s realized cost and ledger data to Inspect’s samples_df(). samples_df() needs pandas and pyarrow, which Inspect Swarm does not install:
pip install "pandas>=2.1.0" "pyarrow>=10.0.1"
This example uses a task with a scorer named match. Replace score_match with your task’s score column (score_<scorer name>):
from inspect_ai.analysis import SampleSummary, samples_df
from inspect_ai.scorer import value_to_float

from inspect_swarm.analysis import SwarmColumns

df = samples_df("logs", columns=SampleSummary + SwarmColumns)
df = df[~df["swarm_resumed"]]
df["score"] = df["score_match"].map(value_to_float(), na_action="ignore")
df.groupby("log")[["score", "swarm_cost"]].mean()
The columns:

swarm_cost: the sample’s priced cost in dollars, from its model_usage, including scorer calls. Tokens are in SampleSummary’s total_tokens.
swarm_complete: no call is known to be missing from swarm_cost. The ledger marks the swarm’s interval complete, and every model in the sample’s model_usage is priced. Calls outside the swarm, including scorer calls, are not checked. False for a sample with no ledger.
swarm_members: members in the roster.
swarm_resumed: the sample resumed from a checkpoint, so the swarm restarted its caps from zero. Swarms now refuse checkpointing (Restrictions), so only logs from earlier versions can have it true. False for a sample with no ledger.
swarm_cost_cap, swarm_token_cap, swarm_time_cap: the swarm’s caps. The time cap is in seconds.
swarm_errored, swarm_no_usage, swarm_unpriced: model calls in the swarm that errored or were cancelled (retries included), that completed with no usage, and whose usage has no cost. Each makes the cost a lower bound.
swarm_unpriced_models: models with tokens and no cost, from the ledger and the sample’s model_usage, as a JSON list.

The columns read from the ledger are null for a sample with no ledger. A sample that runs two swarms keeps only the last one’s ledger, while its model_usage covers both. The columns read the sample’s store and model_usage, so do not exclude either with samples_df(exclude_fields=...).
The columns hold no per-member data. swarm_ledger() reads a sample’s whole ledger as a SwarmLedger, whose members are MemberLedgers with a Meter and Calls each. All are in inspect_swarm.analysis, and SwarmLedger.model_json_schema() describes every field. For example, each member’s cost:
from inspect_ai.log import read_eval_log

from inspect_swarm.analysis import swarm_ledger

log = read_eval_log("logs/my-eval.eval")
for sample in log.samples or []:
    ledger = swarm_ledger(sample)
    if ledger is not None:
        for m in ledger.members:
            print(sample.id, sample.epoch, m.name, m.meter.cost)
The metrics have no reader of their own; read them from sample.store["inspect_swarm:metrics"].

budget is the Budget as given. caps are the caps the swarm applied, derived from the sample’s limits or given: cost in dollars, tokens, and time in seconds, null for no cap. sample_limits are the sample’s limits when the swarm started.
members has one entry per member, in roster order. status is as in How a member ends, null for a member never started. cancelled means the swarm or the sample cancelled the member, so calls it had in flight are unknown. A hard stop during a background drain also sets cancelled; the agent’s returned status is kept. background_started counts the tasks the member started with background(), and background_cancelled those cancelled before they finished, whose calls in flight are unknown too.
meter is the usage and cost of what a member did. suspended_cost is the part spent while token counting was suspended, such as approval calls.
calls counts model calls: calls completed ones other than cache replays, cache_replays replayed from cache at no charge, errored attempts that errored or were cancelled (retries included), no_usage completed with no usage, and unpriced completed with usage but no cost.
runtime meters the controller’s own calls, final the final step’s (the default first-submission answer makes none), and swarm everything in the swarm: members, runtime and final step. The top-level calls counts every call in the swarm. unpriced_calls_recorded counts the unpriced calls the swarm’s meter recorded.
sample_delta is the sample’s usage while the swarm ran. unattributed is sample_delta minus swarm: usage no meter holds, such as the tokens of approval calls.
unpriced_models are models with tokens but no cost. native_compaction_classes are loaded model classes that can compact a conversation natively, which logs nothing, so their usage may be missing.
overshoot is how far usage went past each cap, for caps it passed. Calls in flight at a stop can carry usage past a cap.
stop_reason is why the swarm stopped itself: a controller’s submitted or all_done (as leaderless returns), verified or quiescence, controller:<reason> for any other reason a controller returns, swarm_cap or swarm_time. ended_by is what ended it from outside: sample_limit:<type>, operator for an interrupt, or unknown. Each is null when it did not happen. Both are set when a sample limit ends the swarm during its own stop.
interrupted means an error (a member’s, the controller’s or the final step’s) or a cancellation ended the swarm before it finished, final_cancelled that the final step was cancelled, and resumed that the sample resumed from a checkpoint.
total_complete means no call is known to be missing from the totals: nothing was cancelled or interrupted, every call reported priced usage, and no model class can compact natively. Otherwise the totals are lower bounds. attribution_complete adds that unattributed is zero.

title: Sandboxes
text:
A swarm has one of two sandbox topologies:

Shared, the default: every member works in the sample’s sandbox, at the same time. Members can share files, and can change files under each other.
Per member: each member works in a sandbox environment of its own, and members cannot reach each other’s. What they share goes through a channel, such as the shared-memory board, or a volume every member’s sandbox mounts.

title: Sandboxes
text:
A swarm has one of two sandbox topologies:

Shared, the default: every member works in the sample’s sandbox, at the same time. Members can share files, and can change files under each other.
Per member: each member works in a sandbox environment of its own, and members cannot reach each other’s. What they share goes through a channel, such as the shared-memory board, or a volume every member’s sandbox mounts.

title: Sandboxes
Sandboxes
text:
Per member
With sandbox, a member works in a sandbox environment of its own, which becomes its default, so sandbox() in its tools returns it. {member} stands for the member’s name, so sandbox="{member}" gives each copy of a counted member its own:
from inspect_ai.agent import react
from inspect_ai.tool import bash

from inspect_swarm import member, swarm

solver = swarm(
    members=member(
        react, args={"tools": [bash()]}, name="agent", count=2, sandbox="{member}"
    ),
    channels=[],
)
agent-1 and agent-2 run in the environments of those names. With count=1 the member’s name has no number, so {member} is agent; a task whose member count is a parameter can give each member its own record, [member(..., name=f"agent-{i}", sandbox=f"agent-{i}") for i in range(1, k + 1)], so the names match the environments for every count. The sample’s sandbox configuration provides them (for Docker, a compose service for each), and the swarm checks that they exist when it starts:
services:
  agent-1:
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: tail -f /dev/null
    network_mode: none
    x-default: true
  agent-2:
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: tail -f /dev/null
    network_mode: none

When one member has its own sandbox, every member must have one, and no two can have the same one.
Tools that choose a sandbox without a name, such as bash(), text_editor(), bash_session() and the agent bridge, use the member’s own.
The filesystem channel describes a shared sandbox, so it is refused: pass channels=[], channels=[shared_memory()] for a board the members share, or filesystem(shared_volume=True) for a shared volume.
The preamble tells each member that it works in its own sandbox, which no other member can reach.


Shared services
A member cannot see the sample’s other environments, except those in its visible_sandboxes, such as a service every member uses. It reaches those only by name, as sandbox("comparator"):
member(
    react,
    args={"tools": [bash()]},
    name="agent",
    count=3,
    sandbox="{member}",

    command: tail -f /dev/null
    volumes:
      - shared:/shared
    x-default: true
  agent-2:
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: tail -f /dev/null
    volumes:
      - shared:/shared
volumes:
  shared:
solver = swarm(

title: Sandboxes
text:
Sizing
The two topologies cost different resources:

Shared: one sandbox runs every member’s tool calls at once. Size it for k agents working at the same time, not one: CPU, memory, disk, and process limits. A compose service’s cpus and mem_limit set them for Docker.
Per member: each sample starts k sandboxes, plus any shared services. A sample of 32 members, each with a 32 GiB container, needs 32 such containers at once.

Inspect’s max_sandboxes (for Docker, twice the number of CPUs by default) limits how many samples have their sandboxes running at once, not how many containers they hold. With per-member sandboxes, the containers running at once can reach max_sandboxes × (k + services). Lower max_sandboxes or max_samples to fit the machine or cluster, and keep each member’s container no larger than one agent needs.

title: Sandboxes
text:
Scoring
The task’s scorer runs after the swarm, outside every member, where sandbox() is the sample’s default. A scorer that grades the members’ work names each member’s sandbox, as in sandbox("agent-1"). The result record’s sandbox field says which member used which. See Scoring.

title: Budgets
text:
A swarm takes its budget from the sample’s limits. With the default Budget(), it reads the sample’s cost, token and time limits when it starts and stops its members at 95% of each. The other 5% (reserve) covers calls already in flight when the swarm stops.

)

title: Budgets
text:
Cost data
A cost cap needs cost data for every member’s model. The swarm checks this when it starts and raises an error naming the models that have none. Configure prices with set_model_cost() or --model-cost-config.

title: Budgets
text:
Splits
Budget.split divides the cost and token caps between members:

"pool" (default): members share one budget, and any member may spend all of it.
"equal": each member gets an equal share.
A tuple of weights, one per member in roster order: (1, 1, 2) gives the third member half.

A member that uses up its share stops with status share. Its unused share is not given to the others, so the split stays a fixed condition of the experiment. The swarm’s caps still apply above the shares: when a call reaches a cap and a share at once, the cap wins, and the swarm stops with swarm_cap.

title: Budgets
text:
What members see
When the swarm has a cap, each member’s preamble says how the budget is split. The swarm_resources() tool, as in the example above, lets a member check the swarm’s caps, how much all members have used, and its own share. Code inside a member can read the same with swarm_budget().
A tool that reads sample_limits() shows the sample’s limits, not the swarm’s caps, so it overstates what members can spend.

title: Budgets
text:
Sweeps
Agent count, budget and split are task parameters, so they can be swept. examples/budget_sweep.py:

from inspect_ai.scorer import match
from questions import QUESTIONS

from inspect_swarm import Budget, member, swarm, swarm_resources

def budget_sweep(
    k: int = 4, budget: float = 1.0, split: Literal["pool", "equal"] = "pool"
) -> Task:
